Frequency domain decomposition

Recovering a shape from vibration measurements

Two sensors on a vibrating structure record two time histories. We want to identify a mode shape: the relative amplitudes and phases with which the sensor locations move in one mode. The forces are not measured. What information in the recordings could reveal that shape?

First consider an ideal case in which only one mode contributes. Suppose that, whenever the first sensor moves 1 mm in its positive direction, the second moves 2 mm in its negative direction. Let ttt denote time, a(t)a(t)a(t) the first displacement, and y(t)y(t)y(t) the column vector of both measurements. The fixed vector vvv describes their relative motion:

y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)]=v a(t),v=[1−2].y(t)=\begin{bmatrix}a(t)\\-2a(t)\end{bmatrix}=v\,a(t),\qquad v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}.y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)​]=va(t),v=[1−2​].
(1)

The time dependence is entirely in a(t)a(t)a(t). It can be irregular; the spatial ratio remains 1:−21:-21:−2. In this ideal case, inspecting the two time histories would already reveal the shape. Real measurements contain several modes at once, so that ratio usually changes with time. FDD looks for a fixed pattern within a frequency band, where one mode may dominate.

To see what survives in the frequency domain, let fff denote frequency in hertz, A(f)A(f)A(f) the Fourier coefficient of a(t)a(t)a(t) over a record, and Y1(f),Y2(f)Y_1(f),Y_2(f)Y1​(f),Y2​(f) the corresponding sensor coefficients. Linearity of the Fourier transform gives Y1=AY_1=AY1​=A and Y2=−2AY_2=-2AY2​=−2A. An overbar denotes complex conjugation and vertical bars denote magnitude. At each frequency,

∣Y1∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1Yˉ2=−2∣A∣2.|Y_1|^2=|A|^2,\qquad |Y_2|^2=4|A|^2,\qquad Y_1\bar Y_2=-2|A|^2.∣Y1​∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2​∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1​Yˉ2​=−2∣A∣2.

The separate power spectra preserve the amplitude ratio, but lose the sign: squaring gives the same result for 2A2A2A and −2A-2A−2A. The cross product preserves their opposite motion. This is why we retain the products between channels.

Averaging these products and applying the spectral normalization gives the power spectral density (PSD) matrix Gy(f)G_y(f)Gy​(f). Let Sa(f)S_a(f)Sa​(f) be the PSD of the first signal, its mean-square displacement per unit frequency, and let the superscript TTT denote transpose. For zero-mean stationary records—whose mean is zero and whose expected products depend only on the time separation—the spectral definition below gives

Gy(f)=Sa(f) vvT=Sa(f)[1−2−24].G_y(f)=S_a(f)\,vv^T=S_a(f)\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-2&4\end{bmatrix}.Gy​(f)=Sa​(f)vvT=Sa​(f)[1−2​−24​].
(2)

Where Sa(f)>0S_a(f)>0Sa​(f)>0, this matrix has only one independent column, so its rank is one. Multiplication shows that its eigenvector with nonzero eigenvalue is precisely the measured shape:

Gy(f)v=5Sa(f)v,Gy(f)[21]=0.G_y(f)v=5S_a(f)v,\qquad G_y(f)\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}=0.Gy​(f)v=5Sa​(f)v,Gy​(f)[21​]=0.
(3)

The eigenvalue depends on how strongly the motion is excited. The eigenvector gives the relative motion 1:−21:-21:−2, regardless of that strength. For a rank-one PSD matrix, a singular value decomposition recovers this same direction.

Frequency domain decomposition (FDD) applies this calculation to the measured spectral matrix at each frequency. The remaining task is to establish when a mechanical mode produces an approximately rank-one spectrum, and when other modes or the excitation invalidate that interpretation. [3]

Modes of a mechanical system

Consider a linear mechanical system with nnn displacement coordinates, rrr force inputs, and ppp measured channels. A coordinate is one degree of freedom; a channel is one recorded sensor signal. Let q(t)q(t)q(t), x(t)x(t)x(t), and y(t)y(t)y(t) denote the displacement, force, and measured-displacement vectors.

The real matrices M,C,KM,C,KM,C,K are the n×nn\times nn×n mass, viscous damping, and stiffness matrices, with MMM invertible. The matrices BBB and LLL, of sizes n×rn\times rn×r and p×np\times np×n, distribute the forces and select the measurements. A dot denotes a time derivative. The equations are

Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=Bx,\qquad y=Lq.Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.
(4)

Linearity means that responses add and scale with the inputs; time invariance means that the matrices are constant. The distinction between qqq and yyy matters: a structure may have many coordinates and only a few sensors.

For free motion, set x=0x=0x=0. Physical displacement q(t)q(t)q(t) is real. To find the modes, we temporarily allow a complex auxiliary solution, denoted qc(t)q_c(t)qc​(t). We seek a fixed spatial vector ϕm≠0\phi_m\ne0ϕm​=0, the shape of mode mmm, evolving at a complex rate λm\lambda_mλm​ in inverse seconds:

qc(t)=ϕmeλmt,q˙c=λmϕmeλmt,q¨c=λm2ϕmeλmt.q_c(t)=\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t},\quad \dot q_c=\lambda_m\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t},\quad \ddot q_c=\lambda_m^2\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t}.qc​(t)=ϕm​eλm​t,q˙​c​=λm​ϕm​eλm​t,q¨​c​=λm2​ϕm​eλm​t.
(5)

Substituting into (4) and cancelling the nonzero exponential leaves a matrix polynomial. For a complex rate sss, define the dynamic stiffness matrix Z(s)=s2M+sC+KZ(s)=s^2M+sC+KZ(s)=s2M+sC+K. Writing det⁡\detdet for the determinant, the admissible rates and shapes satisfy the quadratic eigenvalue problem:

Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λm)ϕm=0,det⁡Z(λm)=0.Z(s)=s^2M+sC+K,\quad Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0,\quad \det Z(\lambda_m)=0.Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λm​)ϕm​=0,detZ(λm​)=0.
(6)

The last equality follows because Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​) maps a nonzero vector to zero and is therefore singular. A numerical solution normally uses an equivalent first-order eigenproblem; the state-space derivation is given below. [1]

Solving (6) gives the rates λm\lambda_mλm​. To interpret one of them, return to the time factor eλmte^{\lambda_m t}eλm​t in (5). Let σm\sigma_mσm​ and ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​ be its real and imaginary parts, and let jjj be the imaginary unit, j2=−1j^2=-1j2=−1. Euler’s formula separates the exponential into an amplitude factor and an oscillation:

λm=σm+jωd,m,eλmt=eσmt[cos⁡(ωd,mt)+jsin⁡(ωd,mt)].\lambda_m=\sigma_m+j\omega_{d,m},\qquad e^{\lambda_m t}=e^{\sigma_m t}\bigl[\cos(\omega_{d,m}t)+j\sin(\omega_{d,m}t)\bigr].λm​=σm​+jωd,m​,eλm​t=eσm​t[cos(ωd,m​t)+jsin(ωd,m​t)].

If σm<0\sigma_m<0σm​<0, the amplitude decays; if σm>0\sigma_m>0σm​>0, it grows. A nonzero imaginary part produces oscillation. Since the system matrices are real, nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. Select the member with ωd,m>0\omega_{d,m}>0ωd,m​>0. For a decaying mode, define αm=−σm>0\alpha_m=-\sigma_m>0αm​=−σm​>0, so λm=−αm+jωd,m\lambda_m=-\alpha_m+j\omega_{d,m}λm​=−αm​+jωd,m​. The decay rate is therefore αm\alpha_mαm​, and the damped angular frequency is ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​, in radians per second. The complex solution is a way to represent this motion; it is not a complex physical displacement.

Because the free equations are linear with real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of any complex solution separately satisfy them. Equivalently, a conjugate pair combines into a real modal contribution. Let cmc_mcm​ be a complex coefficient fixed by the initial conditions, qm(t)q_m(t)qm​(t) the displacement contribution of this pair, and Re⁡\operatorname{Re}Re denote real part:

qm(t)=cmϕmeλmt+cˉmϕˉmeλˉmt=2Re⁡ ⁣(cmϕmeλmt).q_m(t)=c_m\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t}+\bar c_m\bar\phi_m e^{\bar\lambda_m t}=2\operatorname{Re}\!\left(c_m\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t}\right).qm​(t)=cm​ϕm​eλm​t+cˉm​ϕˉ​m​eλˉm​t=2Re(cm​ϕm​eλm​t).

The imaginary parts cancel. A complex mode shape records relative phases between coordinates; each coordinate still has a real displacement. Summing these real contributions gives the physical free response q(t)q(t)q(t), with the coefficients chosen to match its real initial displacement and velocity.

Natural frequency and damping ratio

We already know the decay rate and oscillation frequency from the eigenvalue. The terms natural frequency and damping ratio come from a mass–spring–damper system. Consider a mass μ>0\mu>0μ>0, spring stiffness k>0k>0k>0, damping coefficient b≥0b\ge0b≥0, and displacement u(t)u(t)u(t) from equilibrium. With no external force,

μu¨+bu˙+ku=0.\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku=0.μu¨+bu˙+ku=0.

First remove the damper, setting b=0b=0b=0. Dividing by the mass gives u¨+(k/μ)u=0\ddot u+(k/\mu)u=0u¨+(k/μ)u=0. A cosine at angular frequency ωn\omega_nωn​ has second derivative −ωn2-\omega_n^2−ωn2​ times itself, so this equation requires ωn2=k/μ\omega_n^2=k/\muωn2​=k/μ. This is the undamped natural angular frequency: the rate of free oscillation set by mass and stiffness. Its value in cycles per second is fn=ωn/(2π)f_n=\omega_n/(2\pi)fn​=ωn​/(2π).

Restore the damper. Before defining a damping ratio, find the value of bbb at which oscillation disappears. Substituting este^{st}est into the equation of motion and cancelling the exponential gives the characteristic equation: its roots are the allowed exponential rates.

μs2+bs+k=0,s=−b±b2−4μk2μ.\mu s^2+bs+k=0,\qquad s=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4\mu k}}{2\mu}.μs2+bs+k=0,s=2μ−b±b2−4μk​​.

The expression under the square root determines the type of motion. When b2<4μkb^2<4\mu kb2<4μk, the roots are complex and produce oscillation; when b2>4μkb^2>4\mu kb2>4μk, both roots are real and negative, so the motion contains only decaying exponentials. At the boundary, the roots coincide. Denote this critical damping coefficient by bcritb_{\mathrm{crit}}bcrit​. Since b≥0b\ge0b≥0,

bcrit2−4μk=0⟹bcrit=2μk,ζ≡bbcrit=b2μk.b_{\mathrm{crit}}^2-4\mu k=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_{\mathrm{crit}}=2\sqrt{\mu k},\qquad \zeta\equiv\frac{b}{b_{\mathrm{crit}}}=\frac{b}{2\sqrt{\mu k}}.bcrit2​−4μk=0⟹bcrit​=2μk​,ζ≡bcrit​b​=2μk​b​.

The symbol ≡\equiv≡ here introduces a definition. We define the dimensionless damping ratio ζ\zetaζ as the actual damping divided by this critical value. Thus ζ=0.05\zeta=0.05ζ=0.05 means 5% of critical damping; 0<ζ<10<\zeta<10<ζ<1 is underdamped, ζ=1\zeta=1ζ=1 is critically damped, and ζ>1\zeta>1ζ>1 is overdamped. The denominator and its factor of 2 come directly from the quadratic roots. [9]

Using ωn=k/μ\omega_n=\sqrt{k/\mu}ωn​=k/μ​, the damping coefficient per unit mass becomes b/μ=2ζωnb/\mu=2\zeta\omega_nb/μ=2ζωn​. Dividing the motion equation by μ\muμ therefore gives the conventional oscillator equation and its characteristic polynomial:

u¨+2ζωnu˙+ωn2u=0,s2+2ζωns+ωn2=0.\ddot u+2\zeta\omega_n\dot u+\omega_n^2u=0,\qquad s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2=0.u¨+2ζωn​u˙+ωn2​u=0,s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​=0.

Returning to the modal eigenvalue

The link between an eigenvalue and a polynomial root comes from the exponential solution. In the mechanical system, substituting qc(t)=ϕmeλmtq_c(t)=\phi_m e^{\lambda_m t}qc​(t)=ϕm​eλm​t gave Z(λm)ϕm=0Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0Z(λm​)ϕm​=0. Since ϕm≠0\phi_m\ne0ϕm​=0, the matrix is singular: det⁡Z(λm)=0\det Z(\lambda_m)=0detZ(λm​)=0. Thus λm\lambda_mλm​ is both an eigenvalue of the mechanical problem and a root of its determinant polynomial.

For a scalar oscillator the same substitution gives a scalar equation. Denote its characteristic polynomial by p(s)=s2+2ζωns+ωn2p(s)=s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2p(s)=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​. To test whether it admits the rate λm\lambda_mλm​, substitute the auxiliary complex motion uc(t)=eλmtu_c(t)=e^{\lambda_m t}uc​(t)=eλm​t:

u¨c+2ζωnu˙c+ωn2uc=0⟹(λm2+2ζωnλm+ωn2)eλmt=0⟹p(λm)=0.\begin{aligned}\ddot u_c+2\zeta\omega_n\dot u_c+\omega_n^2u_c&=0\\\Longrightarrow\quad (\lambda_m^2+2\zeta\omega_n\lambda_m+\omega_n^2)e^{\lambda_m t}&=0\\\Longrightarrow\quad p(\lambda_m)&=0.\end{aligned}u¨c​+2ζωn​u˙c​+ωn2​uc​⟹(λm2​+2ζωn​λm​+ωn2​)eλm​t⟹p(λm​)​=0=0=0.​

The last step follows because the exponential never vanishes. Therefore the oscillator admits eλmte^{\lambda_m t}eλm​t precisely when λm\lambda_mλm​ is a root of ppp. It is not automatically a root of an arbitrary oscillator’s polynomial. We are choosing an equivalent oscillator whose two exponential rates match the already computed mechanical pair λm=−αm+jωd,m\lambda_m=-\alpha_m+j\omega_{d,m}λm​=−αm​+jωd,m​ and λˉm=−αm−jωd,m\bar\lambda_m=-\alpha_m-j\omega_{d,m}λˉm​=−αm​−jωd,m​.

Its characteristic polynomial must be zero at both rates. The factor s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ is zero at the first, and s−λˉms-\bar\lambda_ms−λˉm​ is zero at the second. Their product is therefore a quadratic with exactly the required roots. We choose its leading coefficient to be 1, as in the oscillator equation after division by mass. For example, roots 2 and 3 give (s−2)(s−3)=s2−5s+6(s-2)(s-3)=s^2-5s+6(s−2)(s−3)=s2−5s+6; the same factorization rule applies to complex roots.

Substitute the two eigenvalues into these factors and expand. Since j2=−1j^2=-1j2=−1, the imaginary terms cancel:

(s−λm)(s−λˉm)=(s+αm−jωd,m)(s+αm+jωd,m)=(s+αm)2−(jωd,m)2=s2+2αms+(αm2+ωd,m2).\begin{aligned}(s-\lambda_m)(s-\bar\lambda_m)&=(s+\alpha_m-j\omega_{d,m})(s+\alpha_m+j\omega_{d,m})\\&=(s+\alpha_m)^2-(j\omega_{d,m})^2\\&=s^2+2\alpha_ms+(\alpha_m^2+\omega_{d,m}^2).\end{aligned}(s−λm​)(s−λˉm​)​=(s+αm​−jωd,m​)(s+αm​+jωd,m​)=(s+αm​)2−(jωd,m​)2=s2+2αm​s+(αm2​+ωd,m2​).​

Matching this with s2+2ζmωn,ms+ωn,m2s^2+2\zeta_m\omega_{n,m}s+\omega_{n,m}^2s2+2ζm​ωn,m​s+ωn,m2​ requires ζmωn,m=αm\zeta_m\omega_{n,m}=\alpha_mζm​ωn,m​=αm​ and ωn,m2=αm2+ωd,m2\omega_{n,m}^2=\alpha_m^2+\omega_{d,m}^2ωn,m2​=αm2​+ωd,m2​. These define the oscillator parameters associated with mode mmm. With ∣λm∣|\lambda_m|∣λm​∣ denoting magnitude,

ωn,m=∣λm∣=αm2+ωd,m2,ζm=αmωn,m,ωd,m=ωn,m1−ζm2.\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|=\sqrt{\alpha_m^2+\omega_{d,m}^2},\quad \zeta_m=\frac{\alpha_m}{\omega_{n,m}},\quad \omega_{d,m}=\omega_{n,m}\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}.ωn,m​=∣λm​∣=αm2​+ωd,m2​​,ζm​=ωn,m​αm​​,ωd,m​=ωn,m​1−ζm2​​.
(7)

The eigenvalue now gives three quantities: αm\alpha_mαm​ describes how quickly the amplitude decays, ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​ describes how fast it oscillates, and ζm\zeta_mζm​ expresses the damping relative to the critical value. The plot below shows how these quantities change together.

How a mode enters the forced response

Free motion identifies the possible rates and shapes. To connect them to measurements under random forcing, we need the transfer matrix.

The Laplace transform converts a differential equation in time into an algebraic equation. Write s=σ+jωs=\sigma+j\omegas=σ+jω, where σ\sigmaσ is a real exponential weighting rate and ω\omegaω is angular frequency. Denote the Laplace transform by L\mathcal LL, and let Q(s)Q(s)Q(s) be the transform of displacement, taken entry by entry:

Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞q(t)e−st dt=∫0∞q(t)e−σte−jωt dt.Q(s)=\mathcal L\{q\}(s)=\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-st}\,dt=\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt.Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞​q(t)e−stdt=∫0∞​q(t)e−σte−jωtdt.

This is a Fourier transform of the exponentially weighted signal on t≥0t\ge0t≥0. Choosing σ\sigmaσ sufficiently large makes the integral converge for signals that grow no faster than an exponential. The variable sss ranges over complex values; the eigenvalues λm\lambda_mλm​ found earlier are particular rates belonging to the system.

The useful property follows by integration by parts. The endpoint term at infinity vanishes in the region of convergence, giving

L{q˙}(s)=[q(t)e−st]0∞+sQ(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),L{q¨}(s)=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙(0).\begin{aligned}\mathcal L\{\dot q\}(s)&=\bigl[q(t)e^{-st}\bigr]_0^\infty+sQ(s)=sQ(s)-q(0),\\\mathcal L\{\ddot q\}(s)&=s^2Q(s)-sq(0)-\dot q(0).\end{aligned}L{q˙​}(s)L{q¨​}(s)​=[q(t)e−st]0∞​+sQ(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙​(0).​

Thus, with zero initial displacement and velocity, each time derivative becomes multiplication by sss. [10] We impose these initial conditions to isolate the response caused by the force input; a response due to initial motion can be added separately.

Let X(s)X(s)X(s) and Y(s)Y(s)Y(s) be the transforms of the force x(t)x(t)x(t) and measured displacement y(t)y(t)y(t). Applying the transform to (4) gives

(s2M+sC+K)⏟Z(s)Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).\underbrace{(s^2M+sC+K)}_{Z(s)}Q(s)=BX(s),\qquad Y(s)=LQ(s).Z(s)(s2M+sC+K)​​Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).

The same matrix Z(s)Z(s)Z(s) appeared in the free-motion eigenproblem. Wherever it is invertible, solve for Q(s)Q(s)Q(s) and substitute into Y(s)=LQ(s)Y(s)=LQ(s)Y(s)=LQ(s). The resulting matrix mapping transformed forces to transformed measurements is the transfer matrix, denoted H(s)H(s)H(s):

Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),\qquad H(s)=LZ(s)^{-1}B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.
(8)

Separating the modal contributions

The transfer matrix contains all the modes at once. To see their individual contributions, we expand it into fractions whose denominators contain one eigenvalue each.

Return to the mass–spring–damper oscillator, now driven by a force F(t)F(t)F(t). Its displacement is u(t)u(t)u(t), and its mass, damping coefficient, and stiffness are μ,b,k\mu,b,kμ,b,k. Divide by the mass and define the input g(t)=F(t)/μg(t)=F(t)/\mug(t)=F(t)/μ, the force per unit mass. With the frequency and damping parameters defined above,

μu¨+bu˙+ku=F(t)⟹u¨+2ζωnu˙+ωn2u=g(t).\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku=F(t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\ddot u+2\zeta\omega_n\dot u+\omega_n^2u=g(t).μu¨+bu˙+ku=F(t)⟹u¨+2ζωn​u˙+ωn2​u=g(t).

Let U(s)U(s)U(s) and G(s)G(s)G(s) be the Laplace transforms of u(t)u(t)u(t) and g(t)g(t)g(t). With zero initial displacement and velocity, transforming gives

(s2+2ζωns+ωn2)U(s)=G(s),U(s)=h(s)G(s),h(s)=1s2+2ζωns+ωn2.(s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2)U(s)=G(s),\qquad U(s)=h(s)G(s),\qquad h(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2}.(s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​)U(s)=G(s),U(s)=h(s)G(s),h(s)=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​1​.

Here h(s)h(s)h(s) maps force per unit mass to displacement. Its numerator is 1 because the normalized input appears with coefficient 1. For a transfer function from the actual force FFF, the numerator would instead be 1/μ1/\mu1/μ.

The denominator is the same characteristic polynomial that determines the free oscillation. For an underdamped oscillator, its two roots are λ\lambdaλ and λˉ\bar\lambdaλˉ. A quadratic with leading coefficient 1 factors as the product of sss minus each root, so s2+2ζωns+ωn2=(s−λ)(s−λˉ)s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2=(s-\lambda)(s-\bar\lambda)s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​=(s−λ)(s−λˉ). Partial fractions then give

h(s)=1(s−λ)(s−λˉ)=1λ−λˉ1s−λ+1λˉ−λ1s−λˉ.h(s)=\frac{1}{(s-\lambda)(s-\bar\lambda)}=\frac{1}{\lambda-\bar\lambda}\frac{1}{s-\lambda}+\frac{1}{\bar\lambda-\lambda}\frac{1}{s-\bar\lambda}.h(s)=(s−λ)(s−λˉ)1​=λ−λˉ1​s−λ1​+λˉ−λ1​s−λˉ1​.

As sss approaches λ\lambdaλ, the first term becomes unbounded while the second stays finite. We call λ\lambdaλ a pole and the coefficient 1/(λ−λˉ)1/(\lambda-\bar\lambda)1/(λ−λˉ) its residue. The pole locates the singularity; the residue specifies its contribution. This decomposition also connects to time: the Laplace transform of eλte^{\lambda t}eλt is 1/(s−λ)1/(s-\lambda)1/(s−λ), wherever the integral converges. Each fraction therefore corresponds to one of the exponential rates found in the free-motion problem.

Now consider one entry of the transfer matrix. Let Hik(s)H_{ik}(s)Hik​(s) map force input kkk to sensor iii. Each entry is a ratio of polynomials: the inverse in H=LZ−1BH=LZ^{-1}BH=LZ−1B has denominator det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s), although factors can cancel. Its partial fractions therefore have the mechanical eigenvalues as their possible poles.

Assume the 2n2n2n roots of det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s) are distinct and form decaying, oscillatory conjugate pairs. Choose one root, λm\lambda_mλm​. In the expansion of HikH_{ik}Hik​, let rik,mr_{ik,m}rik,m​ be the coefficient of 1/(s−λm)1/(s-\lambda_m)1/(s−λm​), and let gik,m(s)g_{ik,m}(s)gik,m​(s) collect the fractions associated with all the other poles, including the conjugate pole λˉm\bar\lambda_mλˉm​. Only the term for λm\lambda_mλm​ is separated out. Then

Hik(s)=rik,ms−λm+gik,m(s).H_{ik}(s)=\frac{r_{ik,m}}{s-\lambda_m}+g_{ik,m}(s).Hik​(s)=s−λm​rik,m​​+gik,m​(s).

This is an exact separation of the sum. The remainder gik,mg_{ik,m}gik,m​ stays finite as sss approaches λm\lambda_mλm​, because its denominators vanish at other, distinct roots. To recover the coefficient rik,mr_{ik,m}rik,m​, multiply by s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ and take the limit:

lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)Hik(s)=lim⁡s→λm[rik,m+(s−λm)gik,m(s)]=rik,m+lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)gik,m(s)⏟0=rik,m.\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H_{ik}(s)&=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}\left[r_{ik,m}+(s-\lambda_m)g_{ik,m}(s)\right]\\&=r_{ik,m}+\underbrace{\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)g_{ik,m}(s)}_{0}\\&=r_{ik,m}.\end{aligned}s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)Hik​(s)​=s→λm​lim​[rik,m​+(s−λm​)gik,m​(s)]=rik,m​+0s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)gik,m​(s)​​=rik,m​.​

The last term tends to zero: it is a vanishing factor times a bounded function. This is why the limit isolates the residue.

Repeat this for every sensor–input pair. Arrange the constants rik,mr_{ik,m}rik,m​ into a matrix RmR_mRm​, and the remainder functions gik,mg_{ik,m}gik,m​ into a matrix Hrest,mH_{\mathrm{rest},m}Hrest,m​, keeping their row and column positions. The entrywise equations become

H(s)=Rms−λm+Hrest,m(s),Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s).H(s)=\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+H_{\mathrm{rest},m}(s),\qquad R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s).H(s)=s−λm​Rm​​+Hrest,m​(s),Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s).

Thus RmR_mRm​ is a constant p×rp\times rp×r matrix, with one coefficient for each of the ppp sensors and rrr inputs. It describes only the chosen pole’s contribution; Hrest,mH_{\mathrm{rest},m}Hrest,m​ contains the others, including the conjugate pole. A zero coefficient means that this particular entry has no contribution from the chosen pole.

Why the residue contains the mode shape

First distinguish the physical shape from the measured shape. The vector ϕm\phi_mϕm​ describes mode mmm at all nnn displacement coordinates. The matrix LLL maps those coordinates to the ppp sensor readings, so define vm=Lϕmv_m=L\phi_mvm​=Lϕm​. For example, if ϕm=[1,3,−2]T\phi_m=[1,3,-2]^Tϕm​=[1,3,−2]T and the sensors measure only coordinates 1 and 3, then vm=[1,−2]Tv_m=[1,-2]^Tvm​=[1,−2]T. The sensors see only that part of the shape.

Why must different force inputs give multiples of this same vector? Let T(s)=Z(s)−1BT(s)=Z(s)^{-1}BT(s)=Z(s)−1B be the transfer matrix from forces to all physical displacements, so Q=TXQ=TXQ=TX. The transfer matrix HHH from (8) maps forces to the sensor readings: since Y=LQ=LTXY=LQ=LTXY=LQ=LTX, we have H=LTH=LTH=LT. Denote the residue of TTT at λm\lambda_mλm​ by WmW_mWm​. From Z(s)T(s)=BZ(s)T(s)=BZ(s)T(s)=B, multiplying by s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ and taking the limit gives

Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s),Z(λm)Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)B=0.\begin{aligned}W_m&=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)T(s),\\Z(\lambda_m)W_m&=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)B=0.\end{aligned}Wm​Z(λm​)Wm​​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s),=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)B=0.​

Thus every column of WmW_mWm​ solves the same equation as the mode shape: multiplication by Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​) gives zero. At the assumed simple root, this nullspace has dimension one, so every such column must be a scalar multiple of ϕm\phi_mϕm​. Let γm,k\gamma_{m,k}γm,k​ be that scalar for force input kkk. The corresponding sensor column is therefore L(ϕmγm,k)=vmγm,kL(\phi_m\gamma_{m,k})=v_m\gamma_{m,k}L(ϕm​γm,k​)=vm​γm,k​.

Now use H=LTH=LTH=LT to return to the measured response. Because LLL is constant, it can be taken outside the residue limit:

Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s)=Llim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s)=LWm.R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s)=L\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)T(s)=LW_m.Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s)=Ls→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s)=LWm​.

Thus the result for the physical residue WmW_mWm​ gives the sensor residue RmR_mRm​, which is the quantity needed in the expansion of HHH.

For example, if two inputs have coefficients 2 and −3-3−3, and the measured shape is vm=[1,−2]Tv_m=[1,-2]^Tvm​=[1,−2]T, their residue columns are

Rm=[2vm−3vm]=[2−3−46]=[1−2][2−3].R_m=\begin{bmatrix}2v_m&-3v_m\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\end{bmatrix}.Rm​=[2vm​​−3vm​​]=[2−4​−36​]=[1−2​][2​−3​].

The columns differ in strength and sign, but both retain the sensor ratio 1:−21:-21:−2. This statement concerns the residue of one pole; the columns of the full transfer matrix need not be proportional because they include other modes.

Keep the two-input example and let X1(s),X2(s)X_1(s),X_2(s)X1​(s),X2​(s) be the transforms of the applied forces, so X(s)=[X1(s),X2(s)]TX(s)=[X_1(s),X_2(s)]^TX(s)=[X1​(s),X2​(s)]T. Multiplying the residue by this input vector combines its two columns:

RmX(s)=[2−3−46][X1(s)X2(s)]=[2X1(s)−3X2(s)−4X1(s)+6X2(s)]=[1−2][2X1(s)−3X2(s)].\begin{aligned}R_mX(s)&=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}X_1(s)\\X_2(s)\end{bmatrix}\\&=\begin{bmatrix}2X_1(s)-3X_2(s)\\-4X_1(s)+6X_2(s)\end{bmatrix}\\&=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}\bigl[2X_1(s)-3X_2(s)\bigr].\end{aligned}Rm​X(s)​=[2−4​−36​][X1​(s)X2​(s)​]=[2X1​(s)−3X2​(s)−4X1​(s)+6X2​(s)​]=[1−2​][2X1​(s)−3X2​(s)].​

Both forces affect the response through the single quantity 2X1−3X22X_1-3X_22X1​−3X2​. The first sensor receives that quantity and the second receives −2-2−2 times it. This is the fixed spatial pattern.

The general notation expresses exactly this calculation. For rrr inputs, collect their coefficients into the row γmT=[γm,1,…,γm,r]\gamma_m^T=[\gamma_{m,1},\ldots,\gamma_{m,r}]γmT​=[γm,1​,…,γm,r​]. Factoring the common vector out of the residue columns gives

Rm=[vmγm,1⋯vmγm,r]=vmγmT,γmTX(s)=∑k=1rγm,kXk(s).R_m=\begin{bmatrix}v_m\gamma_{m,1}&\cdots&v_m\gamma_{m,r}\end{bmatrix}=v_m\gamma_m^T,\qquad \gamma_m^TX(s)=\sum_{k=1}^{r}\gamma_{m,k}X_k(s).Rm​=[vm​γm,1​​⋯​vm​γm,r​​]=vm​γmT​,γmT​X(s)=k=1∑r​γm,k​Xk​(s).

Here Xk(s)X_k(s)Xk​(s) is the transform of input kkk. The product γmTX\gamma_m^TXγmT​X is one scalar because it is a row times a column. In the example, γmT=[2,−3]\gamma_m^T=[2,-3]γmT​=[2,−3]. These coefficients belong to the system; XXX describes the forces actually applied. The appendix derives the coefficients explicitly.

Recall that the residue is only the numerator of the pole term. Its contribution to H(s)H(s)H(s) is Rm/(s−λm)R_m/(s-\lambda_m)Rm​/(s−λm​). Since Y=HXY=HXY=HX, the contribution of this one term to the transformed sensor response is

RmX(s)s−λm=vm γmTX(s)s−λm⏟one scalar.\frac{R_mX(s)}{s-\lambda_m}=v_m\,\underbrace{\frac{\gamma_m^TX(s)}{s-\lambda_m}}_{\text{one scalar}}.s−λm​Rm​X(s)​=vm​one scalars−λm​γmT​X(s)​​​.

The denominator changes the frequency dependence, but it divides every sensor entry by the same number. The relative sensor amplitudes and phases remain those of vmv_mvm​. A nonzero residue has rank one because its columns are all multiples of this vector. [1] [3]

Adding the other poles

So far we have kept only the term for λm\lambda_mλm​. The full transfer matrix also includes its conjugate pole and every other mode. For real system matrices, the residue at λˉm\bar\lambda_mλˉm​ is Rˉm\bar R_mRˉm​. Under our assumption of 2n2n2n distinct roots in conjugate pairs, summing the nnn pairs reconstructs HHH:

Rm=vmγmT,H(s)=∑m=1n(Rms−λm+Rˉms−λˉm).R_m=v_m\gamma_m^T,\qquad H(s)=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+\frac{\bar R_m}{s-\bar\lambda_m}\right).Rm​=vm​γmT​,H(s)=m=1∑n​(s−λm​Rm​​+s−λˉm​Rˉm​​).
(9)

The index mmm runs over the pairs, choosing the eigenvalue with positive imaginary part in each pair. This is the full partial-fraction expansion, not an assumption that one mode dominates.

A mode can be absent from the transfer matrix: if vm=0v_m=0vm​=0, the sensors do not observe it; if γmT=0\gamma_m^T=0γmT​=0, none of the modeled inputs excites it. In either case Rm=0R_m=0Rm​=0, so that root contributes no pole to HHH. [2] Even a visible mode may receive no contribution from a particular force combination for which γmTX=0\gamma_m^TX=0γmT​X=0.

For example, suppose a mode has shape ϕm=[1,0,−1]T\phi_m=[1,0,-1]^Tϕm​=[1,0,−1]T: the first and third coordinates move in opposite directions, while the middle coordinate stays still. If the only sensor measures that middle coordinate, then L=[0,1,0]L=[0,1,0]L=[0,1,0], giving vm=Lϕm=0v_m=L\phi_m=0vm​=Lϕm​=0 and hence Rm=0R_m=0Rm​=0. The mode can be vibrating elsewhere, but this sensor records none of its motion. Moving the sensor to the first coordinate makes this mode visible.

Equation (9) separates the transfer matrix into modal terms. The measured response still contains their sum. We next examine when one term dominates its spectral matrix strongly enough for FDD to recover the shape.

The response spectral matrix

We have expressed the forced response as a sum of modal contributions. In an operational measurement, however, the forces are unknown and fluctuate from record to record. We therefore need a description computed from the sensor signals themselves. The spectral matrix introduced in the opening example does this by averaging products of their Fourier coefficients.

From sensor records to a spectral matrix

Let TTT be the duration of a record and YT(f)Y_T(f)YT​(f) the vector obtained by Fourier-transforming each sensor signal at frequency fff. At one frequency, abbreviate this vector by YYY. For two sensors its entries are Y1,Y2Y_1,Y_2Y1​,Y2​. The superscript HHH means conjugate transpose: transpose the vector and conjugate its entries. It is an operation, distinct from the transfer matrix H(s)H(s)H(s). The outer product is

YYH=[Y1Y2][Yˉ1Yˉ2]=[∣Y1∣2Y1Yˉ2Y2Yˉ1∣Y2∣2].YY^H=\begin{bmatrix}Y_1\\Y_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\bar Y_1&\bar Y_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}|Y_1|^2&Y_1\bar Y_2\\Y_2\bar Y_1&|Y_2|^2\end{bmatrix}.YYH=[Y1​Y2​​][Yˉ1​​Yˉ2​​]=[∣Y1​∣2Y2​Yˉ1​​Y1​Yˉ2​∣Y2​∣2​].

The diagonal contains squared amplitudes. The off-diagonal entries compare the channels. For channels iii and kkk, let θi,θk\theta_i,\theta_kθi​,θk​ be their Fourier phases. Then YiYˉk=∣Yi∣∣Yk∣ej(θi−θk)Y_i\bar Y_k=|Y_i||Y_k|e^{j(\theta_i-\theta_k)}Yi​Yˉk​=∣Yi​∣∣Yk​∣ej(θi​−θk​): conjugation leaves the phase difference. This is the information that distinguishes in-phase motion from opposite motion in our two-sensor example.

For random excitation, the Fourier coefficients vary between records. Write E\mathbb EE for expectation, an average over possible records generated under the same statistical conditions. Averaging YYHYY^HYYH retains the cross-channel products that persist across those records; unrelated phase fluctuations can cancel.

We assume zero-mean, wide-sense stationary measurements: each signal has zero mean and finite mean square, and its expected product with another channel depends only on the separation between the two times. Assume also that a spectral density exists in the band of interest. The response power spectral density (PSD) matrix Gy(f)G_y(f)Gy​(f) is

YT(f)=∫−T/2T/2y(t)e−j2πft dt,Gy(f)=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[YT(f)YT(f)H].\begin{aligned}Y_T(f)&=\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}y(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt,\\G_y(f)&=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[Y_T(f)Y_T(f)^H\right].\end{aligned}YT​(f)Gy​(f)​=∫−T/2T/2​y(t)e−j2πftdt,=T→∞lim​T1​E[YT​(f)YT​(f)H].​
(10)

The factor 1/T1/T1/T converts the squared-transform energy density of a record into a mean-square density. “Two-sided” means that both positive and negative frequencies are included. Integrating a diagonal entry over all frequencies gives that channel’s mean-square displacement, which equals its variance because the mean is zero. A displacement PSD therefore has units of displacement squared per hertz. [5]

In practice, we have finite data, so we estimate this average using windowed segments of a recording. The estimation appendix gives the normalization and averaging procedure.

Why this matrix admits the FDD decomposition

The outer product has two useful properties. Swapping its row and column indices conjugates the entry, so YYHYY^HYYH equals its conjugate transpose. Such a matrix is called Hermitian. Averaging preserves this property.

Next, choose any complex column vector aaa of sensor weights. The scalar aHYTa^HY_TaHYT​ is a weighted combination of the Fourier coefficients. Its squared magnitude cannot be negative, and neither can its average:

GyH=Gy,aHGya=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[∣aHYT∣2]≥0.G_y^H=G_y,\qquad a^HG_ya=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[|a^HY_T|^2\right]\ge0.GyH​=Gy​,aHGy​a=T→∞lim​T1​E[∣aHYT​∣2]≥0.
(11)

This second property is called positive semidefiniteness: every weighted combination has a nonnegative PSD. Together, the two properties ensure that GyG_yGy​ has real, nonnegative eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenvector basis. This is the matrix structure used by FDD.

Connecting the spectrum to the mechanical system

The measured matrix GyG_yGy​ describes the response. To interpret its directions as mode shapes, we must connect it to the transfer matrix derived earlier. For a stable system in stationary operation, its frequency response is H(j2πf)H(j2\pi f)H(j2πf). Define Gx(f)G_x(f)Gx​(f) as the force PSD matrix, using the same Fourier-product convention as (10).

The input–output relation multiplies the force Fourier components by HHH. Consequently, their outer products transform by multiplication on both sides. Suppressing the frequency arguments and writing X,YX,YX,Y for input and output Fourier components, the algebra is

Y=HX⟹YYH=(HX)(HX)H=H(XXH)HH.Y=HX\quad\Longrightarrow\quad YY^H=(HX)(HX)^H=H(XX^H)H^H.Y=HX⟹YYH=(HX)(HX)H=H(XXH)HH.

At a fixed frequency, HHH is determined by the system and does not vary between realizations, so it can be taken outside the expectation. Applying the spectral normalization gives the exact relation

Gy(f)=H(j2πf) Gx(f) H(j2πf)H.G_y(f)=H(j2\pi f)\,G_x(f)\,H(j2\pi f)^H.Gy​(f)=H(j2πf)Gx​(f)H(j2πf)H.
(12)

The force spectrum determines how the system is excited; the transfer matrix contains its modal dynamics. [3] We now substitute the modal expansion of HHH to determine when GyG_yGy​ is dominated by one measured shape.

When the spectrum is approximately rank one

Suppose the force PSD varies little across a resonance. Denote its approximately constant value by QxQ_xQx​. A constant PSD is called white; the matrix need not be diagonal, so different force channels may still be correlated.

Write ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf for angular frequency and let Em(jω)E_m(j\omega)Em​(jω) contain every transfer contribution except the selected pole, including its conjugate partner. Then

H(jω)=vmγmTjω−λm+Em(jω),∣jω−λm∣2=αm2+(ω−ωd,m)2.H(j\omega)=\frac{v_m\gamma_m^T}{j\omega-\lambda_m}+E_m(j\omega),\qquad |j\omega-\lambda_m|^2=\alpha_m^2+(\omega-\omega_{d,m})^2.H(jω)=jω−λm​vm​γmT​​+Em​(jω),∣jω−λm​∣2=αm2​+(ω−ωd,m​)2.
(13)

The selected term becomes large when ω\omegaω is close to ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​ and αm\alpha_mαm​ is small. If it dominates the response to the actual excitation, we can omit EmE_mEm​ in (12). Let dm(f)d_m(f)dm​(f) denote the resulting scalar spectral weight and ≈\approx≈ denote approximate equality:

Gy(f)≈dm(f)vmvmH,dm(f)=γmTQxγˉmαm2+(2πf−ωd,m)2≥0.G_y(f)\approx d_m(f)v_mv_m^H,\qquad d_m(f)=\frac{\gamma_m^TQ_x\bar\gamma_m}{\alpha_m^2+(2\pi f-\omega_{d,m})^2}\ge0.Gy​(f)≈dm​(f)vm​vmH​,dm​(f)=αm2​+(2πf−ωd,m​)2γmT​Qx​γˉ​m​​≥0.
(14)

The numerator is nonnegative: with b=γˉmb=\bar\gamma_mb=γˉ​m​, it is bHQxbb^HQ_xbbHQx​b, a quadratic form of the positive-semidefinite force PSD. The frequency dependence is therefore confined to dmd_mdm​; the direction vmv_mvm​ is fixed. This is the general version of the two-sensor example.

The assumption concerns the excited response, not damping alone. A nearby mode can remain important, and a lightly damped mode may be weakly forced or poorly observed. The residual bound below makes this distinction precise. [3]

Extracting the mode shape

In practice, GyG_yGy​ is replaced by an estimate G^y\widehat G_yGy​, with the hat indicating a quantity computed from data. FDD applies a singular value decomposition (SVD) separately at each frequency. For a Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrix, the singular vectors can be chosen as unit eigenvectors with zero pairwise inner products (orthonormal eigenvectors). The singular values are the corresponding eigenvalues.

At frequency fif_ifi​, let uk(fi)u_k(f_i)uk​(fi​) and sk(fi)s_k(f_i)sk​(fi​) be these vectors and values, ordered largest first. Assemble the vectors into the columns of UiU_iUi​ and the values into the diagonal matrix SiS_iSi​. Then

G^y(fi)=UiSiUiH=∑k=1psk(fi)uk(fi)uk(fi)H,s1≥s2≥⋯≥0.\widehat G_y(f_i)=U_i S_i U_i^H=\sum_{k=1}^{p}s_k(f_i)u_k(f_i)u_k(f_i)^H,\quad s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge0.Gy​(fi​)=Ui​Si​UiH​=k=1∑p​sk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)H,s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥0.
(15)

For a vector vvv, write ∥v∥=vHv\|v\|=\sqrt{v^Hv}∥v∥=vHv​ for its Euclidean norm. The rank-one matrix in (14) has a single nonzero eigenvalue, since

(dmvmvmH)vm=dm∥vm∥2vm.\bigl(d_mv_mv_m^H\bigr)v_m=d_m\|v_m\|^2v_m.(dm​vm​vmH​)vm​=dm​∥vm​∥2vm​.

Let θ\thetaθ denote an arbitrary common phase angle. Normalizing the eigenvector gives

s1≈dm∥vm∥2,u1≈ejθvm∥vm∥.s_1\approx d_m\|v_m\|^2,\qquad u_1\approx e^{j\theta}\frac{v_m}{\|v_m\|}.s1​≈dm​∥vm​∥2,u1​≈ejθ∥vm​∥vm​​.
(16)

The first singular value describes the spectral strength of the mode; the first singular vector estimates its relative amplitudes and phases at the sensors. For the opening example, these are 5Sa(f)5S_a(f)5Sa​(f) and [1,−2]T/5[1,-2]^T/\sqrt5[1,−2]T/5​. The same calculation holds with any number of measured channels. [3]

Neither the absolute shape scale nor the force amplitude is identified. Multiplying the shape by a constant and compensating in the spectral weight gives the same matrix. Consequently, output-only FDD does not determine modal mass, the effective mass associated with a chosen shape normalization.

Peak frequency is not pole frequency

Let fpeakf_{\mathrm{peak}}fpeak​ denote the frequency of a spectral maximum and ωpeak=2πfpeak\omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=2\pi f_{\mathrm{peak}}ωpeak​=2πfpeak​. Even a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillator distinguishes this frequency from ωn\omega_nωn​ and ωd\omega_dωd​. With h(jω)h(j\omega)h(jω) denoting its force-to-displacement transfer function, and modal subscripts omitted, its squared magnitude is given below. The symbol ∝\propto∝ suppresses a frequency-independent factor; under white forcing, the displacement PSD has this same frequency dependence:

∣h(jω)∣2∝1(ωn2−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2ω2,ωpeak=ωn1−2ζ2.|h(j\omega)|^2\propto\frac{1}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+4\zeta^2\omega_n^2\omega^2},\quad \omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=\omega_n\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}.∣h(jω)∣2∝(ωn2​−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2​ω21​,ωpeak​=ωn​1−2ζ2​.
(17)

Differentiating the denominator gives 4ω[ω2−ωn2+2ζ2ωn2]4\omega[\omega^2-\omega_n^2+2\zeta^2\omega_n^2]4ω[ω2−ωn2​+2ζ2ωn2​]; its nonzero root yields the stated maximum when ζ<1/2\zeta<1/\sqrt2ζ<1/2​. At light damping the three frequencies are close, which explains the usefulness of peak picking. Colored forcing, acceleration measurements, and finite spectral resolution can shift a measured maximum further.

Two modes in the same band

Consider two independent modal responses: knowing one leaves the probability distribution of the other unchanged. Let their measured shapes be v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​ and their spectral weights d1,d2d_1,d_2d1​,d2​. Their contributions add:

Gy=d1v1v1H+d2v2v2H.G_y=d_1v_1v_1^H+d_2v_2v_2^H.Gy​=d1​v1​v1H​+d2​v2​v2H​.
(18)

Multiplying by the first physical shape gives

Gyv1=d1∥v1∥2v1+d2v2(v2Hv1).G_yv_1=d_1\|v_1\|^2v_1+d_2v_2(v_2^Hv_1).Gy​v1​=d1​∥v1​∥2v1​+d2​v2​(v2H​v1​).

The second term generally points away from v1v_1v1​. Therefore a singular vector need not equal either physical shape. If both weights are positive and the shapes are linearly independent, the leading two vectors recover their span—the set of their linear combinations. Recovering each mode separately requires more than a rank-two decomposition. [4]

Orthogonal measured shapes, satisfying v1Hv2=0v_1^Hv_2=0v1H​v2​=0, are a special case. They should not be confused with mass-orthogonal physical modes, satisfying ϕ1HMϕ2=0\phi_1^HM\phi_2=0ϕ1H​Mϕ2​=0. The latter does not imply the former. Equal singular values also leave the basis within the corresponding subspace undetermined.

Estimating damping

Enhanced frequency domain decomposition (EFDD) uses the spatial estimate to select the spectrum associated with one mode, then transforms that spectrum into a correlation decay. The selected part is called a spectral bell. Its width contains damping information that a peak location alone cannot supply. [4]

The modal assurance criterion (MAC) measures agreement between two nonzero vectors. Let v^m\hat v_mv^m​ be a reference shape taken near a resonance and uku_kuk​ a candidate singular vector at a neighboring frequency. Their MAC is

MAC⁡(uk,v^m)=∣ukHv^m∣2(ukHuk)(v^mHv^m)∈[0,1].\operatorname{MAC}(u_k,\hat v_m)=\frac{|u_k^H\hat v_m|^2}{(u_k^Hu_k)(\hat v_m^H\hat v_m)}\in[0,1].MAC(uk​,v^m​)=(ukH​uk​)(v^mH​v^m​)∣ukH​v^m​∣2​∈[0,1].
(19)

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds an inner-product magnitude by the product of the norms, so MAC lies between 0 and 1. It is 1 for proportional vectors and 0 for orthogonal vectors; a common complex scale has no effect.

Starting at the reference peak, follow the matching spatial direction outward on both sides. This direction can move between ordered singular vectors when singular values cross. A MAC threshold of 0.8 is a practical starting value, not a universal constant. Stop when the match fails, set unselected bins to zero, and inspect the resulting bell for another mode’s contribution. [7]

A superscript +++ denotes a one-sided PSD, containing only nonnegative frequencies with the positive interior contributions doubled. Let b+(f)b^+(f)b+(f) be the selected bell and Rm(τ)\mathcal R_m(\tau)Rm​(τ) its autocorrelation at lag τ\tauτ, the time separation between two response values. For a discrete calculation, let fsf_sfs​ be the sampling rate, NNN an even transform length, and Δf=fs/N\Delta f=f_s/NΔf=fs​/N the frequency spacing. Write b+[k]b^+[k]b+[k] for the sample at frequency kΔfk\Delta fkΔf, and ℓ\ellℓ for the lag index. Then

Rm(τ)=∫0∞b+(f)cos⁡(2πfτ) df≈Δf∑k=0N/2b+[k]cos⁡ ⁣(2πkℓN),τ=ℓfs.\mathcal R_m(\tau)=\int_0^\infty b^+(f)\cos(2\pi f\tau)\,df\approx\Delta f\sum_{k=0}^{N/2}b^+[k]\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k\ell}{N}\right),\quad\tau=\frac{\ell}{f_s}.Rm​(τ)=∫0∞​b+(f)cos(2πfτ)df≈Δfk=0∑N/2​b+[k]cos(N2πkℓ​),τ=fs​ℓ​.
(20)

The cosine transform combines equal positive- and negative-frequency contributions. Its discrete implementation requires the one-sided scaling described under spectral estimation.

For an isolated mode under the EFDD approximation, the correlation oscillates with a decaying envelope. Let am(t)a_m(t)am​(t) be that positive envelope, A0>0A_0>0A0​>0 its extrapolated initial amplitude, and TdT_dTd​ the full damped period. Here ttt measures elapsed lag. The logarithmic decrement δ\deltaδ is the natural logarithm, denoted ln⁡\lnln, of the amplitude ratio per period. For peaks separated by kkk full periods,

am(t)=A0e−αmt,Td=2πωd,m,δ=1kln⁡am(t)am(t+kTd)=αmTd.a_m(t)=A_0 e^{-\alpha_m t},\quad T_d=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{d,m}},\quad \delta=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{a_m(t)}{a_m(t+kT_d)}=\alpha_m T_d.am​(t)=A0​e−αm​t,Td​=ωd,m​2π​,δ=k1​lnam​(t+kTd​)am​(t)​=αm​Td​.
(21)

The exponential makes the logarithmic ratio independent of the starting time. Define fd,m=ωd,m/(2π)f_{d,m}=\omega_{d,m}/(2\pi)fd,m​=ωd,m​/(2π). Substituting (7) gives δ=2πζm/1−ζm2\delta=2\pi\zeta_m/\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}δ=2πζm​/1−ζm2​​, and hence

ζm=δ4π2+δ2,fn,m=fd,m1−ζm2.\zeta_m=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}},\qquad f_{n,m}=\frac{f_{d,m}}{\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}}.ζm​=4π2+δ2​δ​,fn,m​=1−ζm2​​fd,m​​.
(22)

A fit to several log peak amplitudes is more useful than one ratio. Same-sign peaks are a full period apart; alternating extrema are half a period apart. The fit should exclude initial distortion, late noise, and beating, the slow amplitude modulation from nearby modes. Bell truncation and spectral leakage—the spreading caused by a finite window—can bias the decay, so the damping estimate should be checked across reasonable spectral and fitting settings. [4] [7] [8]

Using the method on measurements

The calculation is short: estimate the full cross-spectral matrix, decompose it at every frequency, inspect the dominant vectors around candidate peaks, and, if damping is needed, select and fit the corresponding correlation decay. The interpretation depends on a few checks.

  • Measurement consistency. Channels must be synchronized, with known units and sensor directions. Arbitrary channel rescaling changes the spatial geometry seen by the SVD.
  • Spectral estimation. Use the same segments and window in every channel pair. Too few averages can produce an artificially small matrix rank. Zero-padding gives a denser frequency grid, not finer resolution.
  • Modal interpretation. A peak with a stable spatial direction is a candidate mode. A sinusoidal force can also produce a rank-one peak; the decomposition alone cannot distinguish the two.
  • Reported quantities. State the sensor coordinates, shape normalization, cross-spectrum convention, and spectral settings. For EFDD, include the selected bell and the fitted lag interval.

An absent peak does not establish an absent mode. The relevant shape may be weakly excited or invisible at the available sensors. These limitations follow from the same input and measurement factors that appear in the transfer matrix. [3]

Appendix: the state eigenproblem

The quadratic problem can be written as an ordinary eigenproblem by including velocity in the state. Let zzz be the 2n2n2n-component state vector, AAA its evolution matrix, and III the n×nn\times nn×n identity. With zero blocks of the same size, the free equations become

z=[qq˙],z˙=Az,A=[0I−M−1K−M−1C].z=\begin{bmatrix}q\\\dot q\end{bmatrix},\qquad \dot z=A z,\qquad A=\begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-M^{-1}K&-M^{-1}C\end{bmatrix}.z=[qq˙​​],z˙=Az,A=[0−M−1K​I−M−1C​].
(23)

Let Ψm\Psi_mΨm​ be a state eigenvector, with upper and lower nnn-component blocks Ψm,1,Ψm,2\Psi_{m,1},\Psi_{m,2}Ψm,1​,Ψm,2​. Substitution of z=Ψmeλmtz=\Psi_m e^{\lambda_m t}z=Ψm​eλm​t gives AΨm=λmΨmA\Psi_m=\lambda_m\Psi_mAΨm​=λm​Ψm​. The upper block requires Ψm,2=λmΨm,1\Psi_{m,2}=\lambda_m\Psi_{m,1}Ψm,2​=λm​Ψm,1​, and the lower block gives

Ψm=[ϕmλmϕm],−Kϕm−λmCϕm=λm2Mϕm.\Psi_m=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix},\qquad -K\phi_m-\lambda_m C\phi_m=\lambda_m^2M\phi_m.Ψm​=[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​],−Kϕm​−λm​Cϕm​=λm2​Mϕm​.
(24)

Thus every eigenvector of AAA has displacement block ϕm≠0\phi_m\ne0ϕm​=0 and velocity block λmϕm\lambda_m\phi_mλm​ϕm​. Its upper block is the physical mode shape and satisfies Z(λm)ϕm=0Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0Z(λm​)ϕm​=0. Conversely, every nonzero solution of this quadratic eigenproblem gives an eigenvector of AAA by stacking those two blocks:

Z(λm)ϕm=0⟺A[ϕmλmϕm]=λm[ϕmλmϕm].Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}=\lambda_m\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}.Z(λm​)ϕm​=0⟺A[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​]=λm​[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​].

Here the double arrow means that either relation implies the other. In the quadratic problem, λm\lambda_mλm​ selects the matrix Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​), and ϕm\phi_mϕm​ lies in its nullspace; it does not satisfy Z(λm)ϕm=λmϕmZ(\lambda_m)\phi_m=\lambda_m\phi_mZ(λm​)ϕm​=λm​ϕm​. To recover a displacement mode shape from a state eigenvector, simply take its first nnn entries.

The two problems have the same 2n2n2n eigenvalues, counting repeated roots according to their multiplicity. Real matrices give conjugate pairs of nonreal roots. A defective eigenvalue has fewer independent eigenvectors than its multiplicity and requires polynomial factors in time; the simple-pole expansion used here excludes that case. [1], §§3.4–3.6.

Damped modal parameters and undamped structural frequencies

There are two different meanings of “remove the damping” here. For the equivalent scalar oscillator, we set its damping ratio to zero while keeping its frequency parameter ωn,m=∣λm∣\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|ωn,m​=∣λm​∣. For the whole structure, we set C=0C=0C=0 in (4) and solve a new eigenproblem. Let Ωr\Omega_rΩr​ and ψr\psi_rψr​ denote an undamped angular frequency and its displacement shape, with rrr indexing the undamped modes. Substituting a sinusoid into the undamped equations gives

Mq¨+Kq=0,Kψr=Ωr2Mψr.M\ddot q+Kq=0,\qquad K\psi_r=\Omega_r^2M\psi_r.Mq¨​+Kq=0,Kψr​=Ωr2​Mψr​.

For a single mass and spring, these two calculations agree: both give k/μ\sqrt{k/\mu}k/μ​. They also agree mode by mode when damping leaves the undamped modes as independent scalar oscillators. More general damping can couple those motions, so a damped mode can combine several undamped shapes. In that case, matching one damped eigenvalue pair to a scalar oscillator does not reproduce the result of removing damping from the whole structure: ∣λm∣|\lambda_m|∣λm​∣ need not equal any Ωr\Omega_rΩr​. Here, “natural frequency of mode mmm” means the parameter ∣λm∣|\lambda_m|∣λm​∣ computed from its damped eigenvalue. [1]

At a simple root λm\lambda_mλm​, let ϕm\phi_mϕm​ and ℓmH\ell_m^HℓmH​ be nonzero right and left null vectors: multiplication by Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​) on the corresponding side gives zero. The residue is defined by the limit

Z(λm)ϕm=0,ℓmHZ(λm)=0,Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s).Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0,\qquad \ell_m^H Z(\lambda_m)=0,\qquad R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s).Z(λm​)ϕm​=0,ℓmH​Z(λm​)=0,Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s).

The cofactor at row iii, column jjj is (−1)i+j(-1)^{i+j}(−1)i+j times the determinant after deleting that row and column. The adjugate adj⁡Z\operatorname{adj}ZadjZ is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. It remains defined at singular matrices and satisfies Zadj⁡Z=adj⁡Z Z=(det⁡Z)IZ\operatorname{adj}Z=\operatorname{adj}Z\,Z=(\det Z)IZadjZ=adjZZ=(detZ)I. Wherever ZZZ is invertible,

A simple root gives rank n−1n-1n−1. The adjugate identities place its columns and rows in the one-dimensional right and left nullspaces. Let cm≠0c_m\ne0cm​=0 be the resulting proportionality constant and dm′d'_mdm′​ the derivative of det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s) at the root. The symbol O((s−λm)2)O((s-\lambda_m)^2)O((s−λm​)2) denotes a remainder bounded by a constant times ∣s−λm∣2|s-\lambda_m|^2∣s−λm​∣2 near that root. Then

adj⁡Z(λm)=cmϕmℓmH,det⁡Z(s)=(s−λm)dm′+O((s−λm)2).\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)=c_m\phi_m\ell_m^H,\qquad \det Z(s)=(s-\lambda_m)d'_m+O((s-\lambda_m)^2).adjZ(λm​)=cm​ϕm​ℓmH​,detZ(s)=(s−λm​)dm′​+O((s−λm​)2).

dm′=tr⁡ ⁣(adj⁡Z(λm)Z′(λm))=cmℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm.d'_m=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)Z'(\lambda_m)\right)=c_m\ell_m^H(2\lambda_m M+C)\phi_m.dm′​=tr(adjZ(λm​)Z′(λm​))=cm​ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​.

Rm=(Lϕm)(ℓmHB)ℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm=vmγmT.R_m=\frac{(L\phi_m)(\ell_m^H B)}{\ell_m^H(2\lambda_m M+C)\phi_m}=v_m\gamma_m^T.Rm​=ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​(Lϕm​)(ℓmH​B)​=vm​γmT​.

In a minimal state realization, every state direction is reachable from the inputs and observable in the outputs, so no state pole is lost from the transfer matrix. Substituting the factorized residue into the conjugate-pair expansion yields

H(s)=∑m=1n(vmγmTs−λm+vˉmγˉmTs−λˉm).H(s)=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\frac{v_m\gamma_m^T}{s-\lambda_m}+\frac{\bar v_m\bar\gamma_m^T}{s-\bar\lambda_m}\right).H(s)=m=1∑n​(s−λm​vm​γmT​​+s−λˉm​vˉm​γˉ​mT​​).

Gy=DDH+DFH+FDH+FFH.G_y=DD^H+DF^H+FD^H+FF^H.Gy​=DDH+DFH+FDH+FFH.

∥F∥2≤ε∥D∥2,∥Gy−DDH∥2≤2∥D∥2∥F∥2+∥F∥22≤(2ε+ε2)∥D∥22.\begin{aligned}\|F\|_2&\le\varepsilon\|D\|_2,\\\|G_y-DD^H\|_2&\le2\|D\|_2\|F\|_2+\|F\|_2^2\\&\le(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)\|D\|_2^2.\end{aligned}∥F∥2​∥Gy​−DDH∥2​​≤ε∥D∥2​,≤2∥D∥2​∥F∥2​+∥F∥22​≤(2ε+ε2)∥D∥22​.​

A small ε\varepsilonε is a sufficient condition for an accurate rank-one approximation. It depends on the force spectrum and modal visibility as well as pole separation. Light damping, ζm≪1\zeta_m\ll1ζm​≪1, where ≪\ll≪ means much smaller than, is not by itself this condition. The bound is a direct consequence of the input–output PSD relation in [3].

Appendix: spectral conventions and estimation

Conjugation order

Some sources define the cross-spectral matrix with YˉYT\bar Y Y^TYˉYT instead of YYHYY^HYYH. Denote that matrix by G~y\widetilde G_yGy​. Then

G~y=GyT=Gˉy.\widetilde G_y=G_y^T=\bar G_y.Gy​=GyT​=Gˉy​.
(31)

Under this convention, (14) becomes G~y≈dmvˉmvmT\widetilde G_y\approx d_m\bar v_m v_m^TGy​≈dm​vˉm​vmT​. The leading vector estimates vˉm\bar v_mvˉm​, so it must be conjugated to recover our shape convention. Both conventions are valid; they must not be mixed.

SciPy, a scientific-computing library for Python, uses conjugate-first ordering in csd(a, b). If y[i] contains channel i, our entry (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) is obtained with csd(y[j], y[i]). [6]

Welch’s estimate

Welch’s method divides a record into possibly overlapping segments, applies the same window to every channel, and averages the spectral products. Detrending removes a fitted mean or trend. A window assigns a real weight to each sample to control the spectral spreading caused by a finite record.

Let NbN_bNb​ be the number of segments, NwN_wNw​ their length in samples, and w[ν]w[\nu]w[ν] the window at within-segment index ν\nuν. Indices bbb and kkk label segments and frequency bins. Write Yb[k]Y_b[k]Yb​[k] for the vector of unnormalized discrete Fourier transform (DFT) coefficients after detrending and windowing. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the DFT efficiently.

For real measurements, the one-sided factor ηk\eta_kηk​ is 2 at interior positive-frequency bins and 1 at DC (zero frequency) and Nyquist (half the sampling rate), when present. At sampling rate fsf_sfs​, the estimate is

G^y+[k]=ηkNbfs∑ν=0Nw−1w[ν]2∑b=1NbYb[k]Yb[k]H.\widehat G_y^+[k]=\frac{\eta_k}{N_b f_s\sum_{\nu=0}^{N_w-1}w[\nu]^2}\sum_{b=1}^{N_b}Y_b[k]Y_b[k]^H.Gy+​[k]=Nb​fs​∑ν=0Nw​−1​w[ν]2ηk​​b=1∑Nb​​Yb​[k]Yb​[k]H.
(32)

Using identical segments and windows preserves the Hermitian positive-semidefinite structure. Each segment contributes at most one independent direction, so the estimated rank cannot exceed NbN_bNb​. Averaging reduces variability between estimates, but does not eliminate a persistent noise or forcing spectrum. [6]

Longer segments improve frequency resolution; more effectively independent segments improve averaging. Overlap does not make segments independent. Appending zeros before the DFT only samples the same windowed spectrum more densely; it does not improve the resolution set by the segment duration and window. [5]

Density units and the inverse transform

The spectra here are densities per hertz. With superscripts (f)(f)(f) and (ω)(\omega)(ω) labeling density per hertz and per radian per second, respectively, the change of variables dω=2π dfd\omega=2\pi\,dfdω=2πdf gives

G(ω)(ω)=12πG(f) ⁣(ω2π).G^{(\omega)}(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi}G^{(f)}\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\right).G(ω)(ω)=2π1​G(f)(2πω​).

For the EFDD inverse transform, halve the one-sided positive interior bins and mirror them to negative frequencies. Keep the DC and Nyquist endpoint weights from (32). An inverse DFT with normalization 1/N1/N1/N must be multiplied by fsf_sfs​ to obtain the discrete correlation in (20). Normalizing by Rm(0)\mathcal R_m(0)Rm​(0) removes an overall scale but does not repair incorrect mirroring. [5]

Additive sensor noise

Let η(t)\eta(t)η(t) denote sensor noise and GηG_\etaGη​ its PSD. If the noise and structural response have zero cross-covariance at every lag, their spectra add: Gy+η=Gy+GηG_{y+\eta}=G_y+G_\etaGy+η​=Gy​+Gη​. Correlated noise introduces additional cross terms. A large singular value can therefore reflect the measurement process as well as the structure.
